title: Lionsgate CEO Wants to See Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Close Soon: ‘Uncertainty and Delay’ Are ‘Not Good for Anybody’
description: Lionsgate CEO Jon Feltheimer voiced support for the stalled Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, which is headed to an antitrust trial to begin
body:
Lionsgate CEO Jon Feltheimer voiced support for the stalled Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, which is headed to an antitrust trial to begin in March 2027.

	While Lionsgate competes with Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. in some areas, including theatrically released movies, Lionsgate also sees both as customers (or potential customers) in other areas. Ultimately, having the Paramount-WBD close as soon as possible is the ideal outcome, according to Feltheimer, speaking on Lionsgate’s quarterly earnings call Thursday.
	

	“Uncertainty is the worst thing for our business, and uncertainty and delay is not good for anybody,” Feltheimer said. “We know David Ellison well. We did his first series, ‘Manhattan,’ some years ago. I can tell you that I was super impressed with him. He loves content.” 


	The Lionsgate chief continued, “I have no reason not to believe that he will be investing very heavily in content, whether it’s a 30-film slate or whether it’s at a bolstered Paramount+, I would say for us… a better-financed streamer, a competitive streamer, will be better for us, better for us in terms of original programming, better for us in terms of selling library. And so that part of it, I think, is a real positive for us.”

	Feltheimer noted that Lionsgate has “already sold [Paramount] a new television show,” without providing details. 

	“We hadn’t been doing that much with Paramount. We hadn’t been doing that much with HBO,” he said. “So I’m already seeing signs of it. I’m already talking to them about potentially co-financing feature films. That would be good for us, and that would be good for the industry. And I would say, overall, the more movies that are in the marketplace, while it’s competitive, it’s good as the rising tide moves all boats up. And so I guess I would say I’m in favor of this transaction, but most importantly, I’m in favor of certainty and getting all of the delay out of it.”

schema.headline: Lionsgate CEO Wants to See Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Close Soon: ‘Uncertainty and Delay’ Are ‘Not Good for Anybody’

title: ‘The Blue Trail’ Director Gabriel Mascaro and Top Brazilian Producer Paula Cosenza Launch Trema, Set First Slate (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Gabriel Mascaro, director of the 2025 Berlinale Grand Jury Prize winner “The Blue Trail,” and top Brazilian producer Paula Cosenza (“Memory House”)
body:
Gabriel Mascaro, director of the 2025 Berlinale Grand Jury Prize winner “The Blue Trail,” and top Brazilian producer Paula Cosenza (“Memory House”) have teamed to create Trema, launched as a Northeast Brazil production powerhouse. Trema is headquartered in Recife, Mascaro’s home city and capital of Pernambuco state.

	Now up and running, Trema is focusing on international co-productions, scripted series and auteur-driven cinema with global reach.
	

	“I am delighted to be able to foster production in Northeast Brazil – the place where I was born, grew up, and have always lived, and where I am proud to have a new company,” Mascaro told Variety just few days before his landmark “The Blue Trail” crowned a landmark awards run with two statuettes at the Brazilian Academy Film Awards, popularly known as the Prêmio Grande Otelo (Denise Weinberg won Best Actress, while Rodrigo Santoro snagged Best Supporting Actor).  “The goal is to transform the symbolic prominence of Pernambuco cinema into concrete infrastructure for production, financing, development, platform partnerships, and talent exchange.”


	A pioneering international co-producer – Cosenza’s credits include Cannes title “Memory House,” “Tropicalia” (seen at Telluride) and Berlin’s “Absence,” all made with international partners – Cosenza will attend the Locarno Film Festival to present Trema and its titles and look for new projects. 

	As for his follow-up to “The Blue Trail” (“O Último Azul”), Mascaro is “very excited to be developing my next movie, while also exploring the possibility of adapting a Brazilian literary work,” he told Variety.
	

	The production will be set up at Trema, which also launches with a powerful slate of titles from established or fast-emerging Brazilian and Latin American talent: “Three Dark Nights,” by Theo Court, produced by Spain’s El Viaje, Chile’s Quijote, Mexico’s Varios Lobos and Trema; “Rafael,” directed by Brazilian João Paulo Miranda Maria (“Memory House”) and produced with France’s Les Valseurs; “Arca,” from Chile’s Matías Bize (“The Life of Fish”), produced by Chile’s Maria Wood Producciones, Potenza Producciones and Trema, and the first film financed by Trema’s own fund that mixes public and private investors; “Paula & Hortencia,” by Brazil’s Joca Georgia Guerra-Peixe, and from Café Royal, Trema and Belladona; “Oásis” a limited series directed by Gabriela Amaral Almeida and Armando Praça, and produced by Trema and top Recife companies Carnaval Filmes and Desvia and co-produced with Coral Europa in Portugal

	All these productions are healthily or nearly fully financed. “We are talking about titles which are going to get made,” Cosenza told Variety, emphasizing the company’s commitment to working both within auteur-driven cinema and in bigger, more popular productions. 

	Trema’s productions run a broad gamut from “100 Days” by Carlos Saldanha, produced by Ventre, Trema, Boipeba, O2 Filmes, Total Post, Good Hand and Disney’s BVI and “A Grande Castração,” by Andre Antonio and Rodrigo Almeida, backed by Surto e Deslumbramento, Zebra, Desvia and Trema.

	The projects see Cosenza and indeed Mascaro working with prior partners: Quijote co-produced “The Blue Trail”; “Arca” producer Patricio Pereira produced Andrés Wood’s Sundance winner “Violeta Went to Heaven,” partnered by Cosenza. 

	Trema is already establishing a direct line between Recife’s industry and the international production scene. Its main aims, however, also take in enrolling Recife’s key craft talent on projects, bringing on the next generation of great filmmakers in Brazil’s Northeast, and attracting shoots to the state. That means incorporating talent from not just Recife or Pernambuco but other parts of the region. Gabriela Amaral, for instance, is from Bahia, just south of Pernambuco; Armando Praça from Ceará. 
	

	“Kleber and I were the first generation that had the privilege of not being forced to move to Rio or São Paulo to gain recognition. Now at a very beautiful moment of a pulsating Brazilian cinema, it is so empowering to bring attention to the huge talent living and working in Brazil’s Northeast,” Mascaro said. 

	“The most important thing is for us to become a hub looking at Brazil’s Northeast, showing how strong regional companies can support big-name filmmakers but also young filmmakers,” he added.   

	Northeastern shoots are being planned. Based on a true crime that occurred at Ceará’s Praia do Futuro, “Oasis” will shoot in Ceará and Pernambuco, said Cosenza. Already, “A Grande Castração” was shot in Recife. “Save the Date,” an independent romantic comedy directed by Cris D’Amatto, filmed in Pernambuco.

	To build on its plans, Trema benefits from several tailwinds. Featured prominently in Kleber Mendonça Filho’s four-time Oscar-nominated “The Secret Agent,” Recife is already home to two of the four Brazilian directors who have recently helped catapult Brazil onto the international stage: Mendonça Filho and Mascaro.  Also from Recife, Marcelo Gomes’ “Joaquim” (2017) played in Berlinale main competition while “Paloma” (2022) won a Chicago Silver Hugo.

	Director of Cannes’ Un Certain Regard winner “The Invisible Life” as well as Cannes main competition contender “Firebrand,” Karim Aïnouz is a native of neighbouring Ceará, whose capital Fortaleza is heavily featured in another Aïnouz Cannes main competition entry, “Motel Destino.” 

	Aïnouz has been actively involved in Ceará training initiatives, as well as having a career deeply intertwined with talent from Pernambuco, including Gomes himself, a longtime collaborator and co-director of Aïnouz’s “I Travel Because I Have to, I Come Back Because I Love You,” which premiered in Venice in 2009. 

	As Variety has noted in an extensive drill-down on the city’s film scene, Recife boasted a vibrant silent cinema movement in the 1920s.  This was resurrected almost from scratch from the mid-90s with Lírio Ferreira and Paulo Caldas’s “Perfumed Ball” (1996), Marcelo Gomes’ “Cinema, Aspirins and Vultures” (2005), a Cannes Un Certain Regard winner, and“I Travel Because I Have to, I Come Back Because I Love You” (2009), which played Venice. 
	

	In late March this year, as part of Lula’s governmental regional incentive program, Pernambuco was granted R$24,6 million ($5 million), with R$20 million ($4 million) coming from the federal government through the FSA and the remainder from the state through Adepe. 

	None of the projects on the company’s slate have received support from the regional FSA fund, Mascaro underscored. “Trema” was not set up as a vehicle to access this funding. Our strategy is much broader,” he added. The fund will fortify other Recife companies, however, consolidating the city’s talent base, all while sharpening its focus on international co-productions. 

	Talk of Pernambuco’s huge talent, moreover, is no pipe dream: It’s a reality. Mendonça Filho noted to Variety this April that five creatives from Pernambuco were awarded Platino Awards for their work on “The Secret Agent”: Tomaz Alves Souza and Mateus Alves for original score; Thales Junqueira for production design and Eduardo Serrano and Matheus Farias for editing. “It only reiterates the notion that you can make great cinema in Recife. It’s crazy that it would even be up for discussion in 2026,” Mendonça Filho said. 

	Editor Farias, also a director, is in competition in Locarno with “The Riverbank,” his directorial feature debut, co-directed with partner Enock Carvalho. Both filmmakers are from Recife, with the city being at the heart of their queer erotic thriller, a sharp social critique that hones into the complex sociopolitical fabric of Recife and the wider Brazil. Older talent from Recife is now moving back to the city, Mascaro noted.   

	Challenges remain, however, including the biggest for Brazil’s film industry at large: Whether Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will remain in office after general elections, held Oct. 4. Victory by Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, would almost certainly spell an end to significant Brazilian federal state support for its industry. 

	At one of his first major public events ahead of the elections, Bolsonaro invited Argentina’s president Javier Milei — who gravely defunded the country’s film-TV institute INCAA — to share his stage, a gloomy forecast of what can lie ahead for the Brazilian cultural sector. 
	

	“I’ve always made films and series in co-production. My very first film, ‘The Samba Within Me,’ a doc feature about a Rio samba school directed by Joca Georgia Guerra-Peixe, was co-produced out of Portugal and Germany. Co-production is something that I like, and I love,” said Cosenza. International co-production, like private-sector investment, will allow films to scale, she added. 

	Such financing lines may also prove invaluable in other ways. “Whether private or public funding or distribution, Paula is working hard to not depend totally on the Brazilian situation,” said Mascaro, referring to the upcoming elections. 

	Almost all of Brazil’s industry is crossing its fingers that this “situation” will not happen.

schema.headline: ‘The Blue Trail’ Director Gabriel Mascaro and Top Brazilian Producer Paula Cosenza Launch Trema, Set First Slate (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Take-Two Interactive Reaches $1.4 Billion in Sales During ‘GTA 6’ Preorder Opening Quarter
description: Video game publisher Take-Two Interactive drew $1.39 billion in sales from April 1-June 30, the quarter during which it opened presales for “Grand T
body:
Video game publisher Take-Two Interactive drew $1.39 billion in sales from April 1-June 30, the quarter during which it opened presales for “Grand Theft Auto 6,” even as the company’s losses widened. 

	During a call with analysts later Friday, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said “GTA 6” had an “exceptional start to pre-orders,” which were open for five days during the quarter, but did not disclose specific sales numbers.


	The $1.39 billion in total net bookings was not broken down by title in the company’s earnings results Friday, but Take-Two noted the number primarily reflected “better-than-expected performance” from the “NBA 2K” and “GTA” franchises. “NBA 2K” net bookings were up 7% and “GTA” rose 3%.
	

	It should be noted that net bookings, a standard earnings metric across the video game industry, are recorded when an order is placed, while Take-Two only calculates revenue based on its actual earned income. Finalized revenue for the quarter came in at $1.53 billion.

	Overall, net bookings were down 3% from $1.42 billion in the prior year’s quarter. Losses for the quarter was $34.1 million compared with a loss of $11.9 million year over year.

	Pre-orders for “GTA 6” launched June 25, one day after Take Two-Interactive’s Rockstar Games revealed pricing for the game would be $79.99 for the standard edition, which can be purchased as a digital or physical (which includes a code in a box rather than a disc) copy. The “ultimate” version will cost $99.99 and include “an exclusive collection of premium vehicles, weapons, apparel, and action threaded across all aspects” of the game.
	

	Take-Two took a $43.4 million impairment charge during the quarter attributed to the “decision not to proceed with further development of an unannounced title in its pipeline from a third-party developer.”

	Wall Street forecast a GAAP loss of earnings per share (EPS) of 21 cents on $1.36 billion in revenue, according to analyst consensus data provided by LSEG. Take-Two reported a GAAP loss per share of 18 cents on $1.39 billion in net bookings. 

	“Our excellent first quarter results reflect the power of our portfolio and disciplined execution across all of our labels,” Zelnick said in a letter to shareholders. “With these positive trends and excitement around the November 19th launch of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI,’ we are reiterating our Fiscal 2027 Net Bookings outlook of $8.0 to $8.2 billion. Looking further ahead, we expect to sustain this new level of scale and generate strong cash flows, setting us on a path to deliver continued growth and long-term shareholder returns.”

schema.headline: Take-Two Interactive Reaches $1.4 Billion in Sales During ‘GTA 6’ Preorder Opening Quarter

title: Werner Herzog to Be Honored at San Sebastián Film Festival
description:
Prolific filmmaker Werner Herzog will receive the San Sebastián Film Festival’s prestigious Donostia Award during its 74th edition in September.

	T
body:
Prolific filmmaker Werner Herzog will receive the San Sebastián Film Festival’s prestigious Donostia Award during its 74th edition in September.

	The German director will be honored at the Spanish festival’s opening gala and will screen his latest film “Bucking Fastard,” following its world premiere at Venice Film Festival. 

	“Over a career spanning six decades, Werner Herzog has become one of the most influential figures in contemporary cinema, building an extraordinary body of work ―around 80 films― shaped by obsession, extreme situations and the contradictions of human nature,” San Sebastián Film Festival said in a statement. “His films, both fiction and non-fiction, are populated by dreamers and conquerors confronted with extreme landscapes and forces beyond their control. Guided by his concept of ‘Ecstatic Truth,’ Herzog advocates a cinema that transcends the mere observation of facts to reveal a deeper, more poetic dimension of reality.”
	

	Regarded as a pioneer of New German Cinema, Herzog’s credits include “Aguirre, the Wrath of God” (1972), “Fitzcarraldo” (1982), “Grizzly Man” (2005) and “Cave of Forgotten Dreams” (2010). He was nominated for a best documentary Oscar in 2008 for “Encounters at the End of the World” and has won prizes at the Cannes, Berlin and Venice film festivals.


	Starring sisters Rooney and Kate Mara, “Bucking Fastard” tells the “unusual story of twins whose extraordinary bond leads them to speak in unison, love the same man and share the same dreams,” according to its official synopsis. 

	The San Sebastián Film Festival will take place from Sept. 18 to 26.

schema.headline: Werner Herzog to Be Honored at San Sebastián Film Festival

title: Luca Guadagnino to Receive Cartier Glory to the Filmmaker Award at Venice Film Festival
description:
Luca Guadagnino will receive the Cartier Glory to the Filmmaker Award at this year’s Venice Film Festival.

	The Italian director, who is premiering
body:
Luca Guadagnino will receive the Cartier Glory to the Filmmaker Award at this year’s Venice Film Festival.

	The Italian director, who is premiering his seven-hour Bernardo Bertolucci documentary “Joie de Vivre” at this year’s festival, is being honored as “a personality who has made a particularly original contribution to the contemporary film industry,” according to a press release. Guadagnino will be presented the award in a ceremony on Sept. 8 before the premiere of “Joie de Vivre.” 
	

	“It might seem like a rhetorical gesture to say I am honored to receive the Glory to the Filmmaker award, but it is the plain truth for many reasons,” Guadagnino said in a statement. “To be honored for one’s craft or life as a filmmaker is an ambition that no one who makes films could ever presume to imagine achieving — especially by joining a group of filmmakers who have received this prestigious honor before me and to whom I owe so much of my development. So, I want to emphasize once again what an honor it is to receive this award, especially from Alberto Barbera and La Biennale di Venezia. Thank you, thank you!”


	Added Barbera: “The Glory to the Filmmaker Award celebrates in Luca Guadagnino an author who has managed to transform his curiosity into a form of creative freedom. Defying alignment with any single school or movement, he has established himself as a global director, capable of working with leading international actors and producers. He has navigated diverse genres — from melodrama to horror, coming-of-age to psychological thriller — while maintaining a consistent and recognizable voice, without ever losing a deeply Italian identity in portraying bodies, settings and history. His is a vital cinema that does not shy away from risk: nomadic, sensual, sophisticated yet widely accessible, where intellectual provocation and emotion, memory and modernity coexist brilliantly. Glory to the Filmmaker honors the originality of a vision that has succeeded in renewing the language of contemporary cinema, celebrating a career that has brought Italian auteurship into a true dialogue with the entire world.”
	

	Guadagnino is no stranger to Venice Film Festival, and most recently presented his film “After the Hunt,” starring Julia Roberts and Andrew Garfield, at last year’s edition. His other credits include “Challengers,” “Bones and All” and “Call Me by Your Name,” and he recently wrapped “Artificial,” a drama about OpenAI founder Sam Altman (played by Garfield) that was dropped by Amazon MGM after they struck a deal with the tech company. The film was then picked up by Neon, which is planning a campaign for the upcoming awards season.

schema.headline: Luca Guadagnino to Receive Cartier Glory to the Filmmaker Award at Venice Film Festival

title: Bella Thorne Is Also Directing and Writing the ‘Spring Breakers’ Sequel She’s Starring In: ‘From Start to Finish, It’s Lit as F—’
description: Bella Thorne is about to go full “Spring Breakers.” The former Disney star has revealed that in addition to starring in an upcoming sequel to Harmon
body:
Bella Thorne is about to go full “Spring Breakers.” The former Disney star has revealed that in addition to starring in an upcoming sequel to Harmony Korine’s 2012 cult classic, she’s also directing and writing the film.

	Variety exclusively announced the sequel and its cast in May 2025, which also includes “Stranger Things” breakout Grace Van Dien, Ariel Martin (“Zombies 2”) and True Whitaker (“I Love L.A.”). At the time, “Freeway” helmer Matthew Bright was attached to direct, but Thorne said in an interview on Alex Cooper’s “Call Her Daddy” podcast that she has now stepped into the director’s chair.
	

	“The producers watched ‘Color Your Hurt,’ which is the movie that I just wrapped, an early cut of it. And they asked me to write something to see if they would like it,” Thorne said. “And they loved it! And now I’m writing and directing ‘Spring Breakers 2.'”


	“Color Your Hurt” is Thorne’s directorial debut, described as a coming-of-age thriller that follows a young gay man seeking acceptance in a hostile community. Production wrapped on the film in October. 

	Asked how her sequel will differ from the original, Thorne said that 2012 was “such an exploitative time and everyone was going through it,” adding that herself and fellow Disney kids Miley Cyrus, Zendaya and Selena Gomez — the last of which starred in the original “Spring Breakers” alongside Vanessa Hudgens, Ashley Benson and James Franco — were all “being compared of who was going to be that next bad girl.”

	“This time, things are different,” Thorne said. “They are crazy. There’s a lot of craziness, there’s a lot of litness. There is so much litness in this movie.” 
	

	She added that “Spring Breakers 2” involves some of the original team, including Muse Productions’ Chris Hanley (“American Psycho,” “The Virgin Suicides”) and Jordan Gertner (“Bully”). Korine is not involved, and has previously said he has “no interest” in the sequel.

	“I don’t want to get in trouble, but what I can say is it is so litty, litty McTitties,” Thorne teased. “From start to finish, it’s lit as fuck. We are having fun. If you want to go to the theater and have fun, you’re going to have fun with this movie, that’s for sure.”

	Watch Thorne’s full “Call Her Daddy” interview below.

schema.headline: Bella Thorne Is Also Directing and Writing the ‘Spring Breakers’ Sequel She’s Starring In: ‘From Start to Finish, It’s Lit as F—’

title: Danny DeVito-Produced Heist Comedy ‘Drag’ Boards Blue Finch Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Blue Finch Films has taken on international sales rights, outside North America, for the heist thriller comedy “Drag” from directors Greg Yagolnitze
body:
Blue Finch Films has taken on international sales rights, outside North America, for the heist thriller comedy “Drag” from directors Greg Yagolnitzer and Raviv Ullman. 

	The U.K. sales and distribution company plans to launch the title at the market during the Toronto Film Festival.

	Danny DeVito, Lucy DeVito and Jake DeVito produced the film, which premiered at SXSW 2026 to critical acclaim. Briarcliff Entertainment picked up North American distribution rights and is scheduled to open the film in U.S. theaters on Jan. 29, 2027.
	

	The film stars Lizzy Caplan, Lucy DeVito, John Stamos and Christine Ko. Since its SXSW debut, “Drag” has continued its festival run with screenings at BiFan, Fantasia and Tubi FrightFest London.


	The story follows two sisters with a strained relationship who target a house in rural upstate New York for a burglary. The heist goes wrong when one sister injures her back and ends up trapped on the second floor, setting off an increasingly frantic bid to get out before the homeowner comes home.

	“Drag” represents the first independent feature to come out of Jersey Films 2nd Avenue, the DeVito-founded production banner behind the animated FXX series “Little Demon” and the Prime Video sports docuseries “Game 7.” The label’s mission emphasizes distinctive creative voices and stories that defy genre convention.

	Blue Finch Films’ current sales slate also includes the Toronto Midnight Madness selection “Kick On,” the Fantasia titles “Attack On Paradise” and “Unholy Night,” and “Mission,” which is backed by BBC Film and Screen Scotland and stars George MacKay.

schema.headline: Danny DeVito-Produced Heist Comedy ‘Drag’ Boards Blue Finch Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Claes Bang Plays a Masseur of Nazi Leader Heinrich Himmler in ‘I Is Another’ — but John Paul in ‘Bad Sisters’ Is Still One of His ‘Worst Characters’
description:
Claes Bang plays Heinrich Himmler’s personal physical therapist in Locarno premiere “I Is Another.”

	Directed by Felix Randau, it focuses on the tr
body:
Claes Bang plays Heinrich Himmler’s personal physical therapist in Locarno premiere “I Is Another.”

	Directed by Felix Randau, it focuses on the true story of Felix Kersten. Kersten, who passed away in 1960, claimed to have saved numerous lives during the war due to his influence over the Nazi leader. However, many have disputed his claims. 

	“It’s quite a wild story and for some reason it’s never been told,” Bang tells Variety. 
	

	“One of the worst characters I have embodied is probably John Paul in ‘Bad Sisters’ [the Apple TV+ series created by Sharon Horgan]. But I will always try to find something in there that I can relate to. With John Paul, it was his desire to protect his family and his belief that the other sisters were out to get him.” 


	With Kersten, it’s his search for validation.

	“He was trying to get the Nobel Peace Prize! He wanted people to say: ‘You were a good guy.’ It’s something I recognize, because I want people to like my work. I want people to go: ‘Wow, Claes, what you did in that play or that movie was really great.’ To some degree, we all want that. But it became his downfall.”

	In the film – sold by Beta Cinema and produced by Ostlicht Filmproduktion – an ambitious journalist (Valerie Pachner) wants to expose his lies. But she’s also hiding a few secrets of her own. 

	“There were definitely people who were alive at the end of the war that would not have been alive had it not been for him. The problem is, he thought he hadn’t received enough credit for his actions, so he exaggerated them.”
	

	“I like it when a character’s actions don’t match what they present to the world. ‘The Square’ was a perfect example of that.” 

	In Ruben Östlund Palme d’Or winner – and his breakout role – Bang played a respected curator whose perfect life starts to unravel after his phone is stolen.

	“He saw himself as a really good guy. He’s trying to put on this exhibition that’s supposed to say something about humanity, and then he goes and sends threatening letters to people. It makes me wonder: Why do we need that kind of validation? Why do we want fame, or for everyone to applaud us?”

	Kersten’s story and his ties to the Nazis made him a complicated historical figure. But Bang calls for compassion, not judgement. 

	“I don’t think anyone can understand the terror you felt when you got a call to show up at the SS headquarters,” he notes. 

	“If you didn’t obey, your whole family would be dragged out into the street and executed. He didn’t ask for this. Up until this point, he wasn’t a member of the Nazi party or had anything to do with the Nazis when he was summoned to meet Himmler.”

	Kersten became valuable when he was able to help Himmler with the severe stomach pains that had plagued him all his life. 

	“What goes through your heart and your mind when you get a call to go and be part of it? In [another Apple series] ‘The New Look,’ I played a man who was the intermediary between the Nazi party and Coco Chanel. It’s a dark chapter in her story,” he adds.

	“Chanel is a French icon and Juliette Binoche [who played her] wanted to do her justice – she didn’t want to just hang her out to dry. That was one of the things we talked about: What did people know about the Nazi party’s atrocities when they were also keeping them a secret? People were just trying to survive while their country was at war.” 

	He says: “It’s easy to say: ‘When Himmler offered him the job of being his masseur, why didn’t he just say no?’ But we can’t possibly fathom being in that situation.”

	“There’s evidence that Kersten helped people escape, but he was unhappy that, for example, he wasn’t mentioned in Count Bernadotte’s book [about the war]. He wanted to correct it and that got him into trouble.”
	

	It also confirmed his official affiliation to the SS. 

	“It’s quite interesting when in the film, he realizes he’s now a part of it. O.K, I’m Heinrich Himmler’s masseur. Can I make something out of this that will actually do some good? I like when he asks: ‘How many human lives is a membership of the SS worth?’ Even though it’s impossible to answer.”

schema.headline: Claes Bang Plays a Masseur of Nazi Leader Heinrich Himmler in ‘I Is Another’ — but John Paul in ‘Bad Sisters’ Is Still One of His ‘Worst Characters’

title: Starz Revenue Declines 4% in Q2 as Streaming Stabilizes, Company Takes $147 Million Charge Related to Ending Universal Output Deal
description: Starz saw total revenue slide again in the second quarter of 2026 — but the media company reported its first year-over-year growth in streaming reve
body:
Starz saw total revenue slide again in the second quarter of 2026 — but the media company reported its first year-over-year growth in streaming revenue in 18 months. Company execs believe the business is turning around, and they’ve raised their outlook for adjusted OIBDA (operating income before depreciation and amortization) growth for full-year 2026 from low single-digits to mid single-digits.

	Total revenue in the second quarter was $307.9 million, down 4% year over year. OTT revenue as reported was $221.3 million, up ever so slightly from $221.1 million in the year-earlier period. However, Starz said, streaming revenue would have increased 1.4% in the June 2026 quarter excluding $3 million of OTT revenue related to Canadian operations that was recorded in Q2 2025. (Starz transitioned its Canadian operations from a distribution partnership with Bell to a content-licensing model at the end of 2025.)
	

	Linear TV and other revenue declined 14% to $86.6 million. In the second quarter, Starz saw a revenue decline of $13.2 million “resulting from the continued decline in traditional linear households,” per its quarterly SEC filing. That was partially offset by an increase in distribution and other revenue of $1.1 million related to the switch to a content-licensing model in Canada.


	Net loss ballooned to $189.4 million, compared with a loss of $42.5 million in Q2 2025. Starz reported an operating loss of $175.5 million (vs. $26.9 million a year earlier).

	Taking a big bite out of Starz’s earnings: The company took a restructuring charge of $147 million in the second quarter of 2026 in association with the termination of its pay-2 film output agreement with Universal Pictures in April. The wind-down of the Universal deal was previously announced by Starz president and CEO Jeff Hirsch, who cited “lower viewership than we originally projected.” In prepared remarks Friday, Starz CFO Scott Macdonald said, “We continue to expect this to be the final content restructuring charge of this magnitude going forward, which sets the company up for meaningfully lower restructuring activity from here.” Given the timing of Starz’s final cash payments to Universal in 2028, Macdonald said, “we believe 2029 is shaping up to be a significant year for free cash flow growth relative to the trajectory we see across 2026 through 2028.”
	

	In Q2, Starz’s stop-performing titles were the finale of “Outlander”; the premiere of “Power Book III: Raising Kanan” Season 5 (pictured above); and “The Housemaid,” Lionsgate’s psychological thriller starring Amanda Seyfried and Sydney Sweeney, which debuted April 1 on Starz.

	In prepared remarks, Hirsch said “Raising Kanan” Season 5 grew its audience from the first season five years ago, “a rare achievement in today’s television landscape.” In addition, he said, the July 31 premiere of “Fightland,” the boxing crime drama series produced by 50 Cent, was Starz’s No. 2 best-rated original IP launch of all time (after the Season 1 premiere of “BMF” in 2021).

	“Our second-quarter results reflect the momentum we are building across the business and the strength of our content portfolio,” Hirsch said in a statement. “We delivered another quarter of strong audience engagement and OTT revenue growth, and the success of the ‘Fightland’ premiere validates our ownership strategy.”

	Hirsch said the company’s improved visibility into the second half of the year and the early performance of “Fightland” have served to “increase our confidence that 2026 is shaping up to be a more significant inflection year for Starz than we initially anticipated.”

	During the second quarter, Starz launched a new partnership with NBCUniversal’s Peacock that makes Starz available as an add-on subscription to the platform for the first time. And last week, Starz announced a new discounted bundle with Crunchyroll on Prime Video.

	Upcoming programming coming to Starz includes the return of “P-Valley,” the continued expansion of the “Outlander” universe through “Blood of My Blood” Season 2, and the upcoming biopic “Michael” following its record-breaking theatrical run. Further out, Hirsch said, “we continue to build our owned content pipeline beyond ‘Fightland’ with the ‘Untitled Black Rodeo Show,'” which is starting production this month. and several other Starz-owned projects in development.

	Adjusted OIBDA was $60 million for the quarter, ahead of Starz’s expectations and up from $33.4 million in the year-ago period. The company expects Q3 adjusted OIBDA to be in the mid-$30 million range. That “will be our lowest quarter of the year due to higher programming amortization” from the airing of “Raising Kanan” S5, “Fightland” S1 and “Blood of My Blood” S2 all during Q3, according to Macdonald. Starz expects Q4 to “finish the year strongly in the mid-60s.” As such, the company is raising 2026 adjusted OIBDA growth guidance from low single-digits to mid single digits, “and we remain confident in achieving our 20% adjusted OIBDA margin target in the back half of 2027,” the CFO said.
	

	In the second quarter, Starz’s unlevered free cash flow was negative $15 million and equity free cash flow was negative $33 million “given the timing of content payments,” Macdonald said. Free cash flow still came in ahead of expectations, he added.

	Cash content spend was $182 million for the second quarter. With the exit of the Universal agreement, Starz expects to report full-year 2026 cash content spend below $600 million.

	Net debt was $566 million as of June 30, 2026, and adjusted OIBDA leverage ratio was 2.9 times. Starz has obtained commitments to increase its credit facilities by $100 million, comprised of a $67 million increase to its Term Loan A and a $33 million increase to its revolving credit. Even after incorporating the additional $67 million of debt, Starz continues to expect to end 2026 with adjusted OIBDA leverage of approximately 2.7 times.

title: Locarno’s Match Me! Projects Push New Voices, Timely Relevance and Authenticity as a Younger Generation Moves Center Stage
description: Arthouse movies are increasingly made for younger audiences who are replacing ageing stay-at-home baby boomers at Europe’s upscale cinema theaters.
body:
Arthouse movies are increasingly made for younger audiences who are replacing ageing stay-at-home baby boomers at Europe’s upscale cinema theaters. That impact is now working its way through new arthouse projects, seen at Locarno’s 2026 Match Me!, its vibrant co-production meet this year welcoming projects from Europe and Latin America, where a younger generation move center stage or featue at least as co-protagonists. 

	Later this Festival, a comment on market trends. For the moment, a close look at the producers attending Match Me! and a top project they are brining to market: 
	

	BrazilAmadeu Alban, MoviocaBehind “Drag Me as a Queen” (NBCUniversal/E!), the first Brazilian reality show exported globally with formats in the Netherlands and Germany, Alban notes, and doc feature “Anatomy of Chaos,” a current Brazilian box office hit.

	At Match Me! with “The Girl Who Bled Woman” where Dinha, 13, is forced to marry her older sister’s widower, the marriage only being consummated after her first menstruation. Dinha battles to hide her body changes. A coming-of-age drama/survival thriller. 

	Amina Sophia Nogueira, Capivara MoviesWith a 20-year career, taking in a decade as Globo’s talent manager, now developing her first features at Capicara, founded 2024, including “The She-Devil.” Set in working-class Rio de Janeiro during the booming ‘90s, Araí, 11, develops an obsession with an imaginary killer who attacks girls in their neighborhood, while adoring Iara, an aunt who offers guidance and inspiration through her transgressive way of living. Emerging voices Clara Ferrer and Tainá Bevilacqua direct.

	Chile
	

	Francisco Gallardo Soto, EquecoBehind “Designation of Origin,” a 2025 B.O. phenom in Chile from Tomás Alzamora (“Little White Lie”) and now “The Chilean,“ playing Locarno’s Piazza Grande, a sign of its perceived broad audience appeal. At Match Me! with “Falling Waves,” set in a remote southern Chile fishing community where a teen girl’s secret entwines with environmental catastrophe. Suggesting “how guilt, faith, and reality begin to blur as the sea rots under the weight of an environmental collapse,” Reyes tells Variety.

	Catalina Miles, VillanoProducer of “The Red Hangar,”a Malaga and Guadalajara top winner and sales hit, now at Locarno with “Champ,” from Pelayo Lira, behind Ventana Sur/Sanfic WIP “Kingdoms,” a millennial generation portrait. “Champ” is set in Chile, 2000. Samuel, 11, battles to enter an elite school after moving to a wealthy area. But in the race for success, he soon learns, every victory demands a sacrifice of identity.

	Denmark

	Mikkel Smidt, Napkin ProductionsFounded in 2025 by six producers from the same The National Film School of Denmark’s graduation class, pooling experience from Zentropa, Nordisk Film and Danish Documentary. Moving at Match Me! Its first feature film, Mone Frogg’s intriguing mystery drama “Glossy Pictures”: When a son brings his volatile, gambling-addicted mother to an isolated hotel, a casino jackpot and a sudden death pull him into an investigation that unravels everything he thought he knew about his mother.

	Giulia Triolo, Snowglobe A key European producer and co-producer involved in a dazzling lost of films from top filmmakers in Scandinavia, Latin America and beyond, such as Hlynur Pálmason (“Godland”), Joachim Trier (“The Worst Person in the World”), Gabriel Mascaro (“Divine Love”) and Christian Mungui’s 2026 Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Fjord”).  At Locarno with “Grasshoper,” turning on isfit Luka (15, she/they), a summer intern who finds in the blackberry-stained lips of curly-haired Frida — a tentative first love — a sense of belonging and path to their future.

	Dominican Republic

	Pablo Lozano, Sky Films



	

					‘Gagá’
									Courtesy of Sky Films
	



	Sky Films, founded by Pedro García and Rafael Llaneza, counts among its highlights the award-winning Berlinale screener “Ramona” and “The Godfather Part II” documentary “From Sicily to Santo Domingo.” At Locarno with “Gagá,” a documentary currently in post that follows Geo, a white Dominican, and Britis, a Black Haitian-Dominican — spiritual leaders, brothers of the road and keepers of sacred knowledge. “[B]ound since youth by an initiation the state doesn’t recognize, [they] embody the kinship that nationalist politics is working to erase,” says Lozano.

	Isaac Morantus, El Güeso Films
	



	

					‘Camina Ven’
									Courtesy of El Güeso Films
	



	Headed by Isaac Morantus and by Viviana Sánchez, El Güeso Films focuses on stories deeply rooted in Dominican culture but characterized by emotionally universal narratives. Recent works include Sánchez’s award-winning “Nueva Forma” and Morantus’ short “Camina Ven,” which he is now adapting into a feature film. The buddy road trip movie follows a young man seeking to confess his love to a girl before it’s too late. “‘Camina Ven’ is about finding the courage to speak before regret becomes permanent,” Morantus says.

	Estonia

	Inger Põder, Homeless Bob Production



	

					‘Beyond the Visible Flowers’
									Credit: Gabriela Urm
	



	Known for bold artistic choices, original stories, and auteur cinema, it says, such as Rainer Sarnet’s Tribeca title “November” and Locarno splash, the “zany” “The Invisible Fight.” One of her Match Me! Projects: “Beyond The Visible Flowers,” where Anna investigates Paradise, a closed community where her mother shelters from her father, a PTSD victim during the Soviet-Afghan war. “The film examines how what happened in the war 35 years ago has affected one family today,” says writer-director Jaanika Arum.

	Laura Raud, Nafta Films



	

					‘Think of Something Nice’
									Courtesy of Nafta Films
	



	Founded in Tallinn in 2009, one of the Baltics’ biggest production companies, producing and providing services from offices in all three Baltic countries. Behind “Melchior the Apothecary.” At Locarno with “Think of Something Nice” (aka “The Bicycle Thief”), about Sigrit, 10, living in a small town. She receives a new bicycle for her birthday, only for it to be stolen the next day. The film’s central bilingual family is tender, funny, damaged and morally ambiguous, often all at once,” says Raud.

	Finland

	Hadi Nikzad, Lumina FilmsHelsinki-based Lumina Films, founded by Hadi Nikzad, focuses on character-driven, socially resonant arthouse cinema with international potential while also moving into genre. Recent titles include “The Lightning Rod,” selected for Cannes La Cinef, and Jussi Award winner “My Name Is Hope.” At Match Me! with “DOR,” a paranoid thriller about an Iranian-Finnish novelist in Helsinki who suspects she is being surveilled. “[W]hat interests me in ‘DOR’ is not the machinery of surveillance but what it does to intimacy,” Nikzad tells Variety.

	Pilvi Waltzer, BufoDescribed as an “ambitious and thrill-seeking company” and headed by Misha Jaari and Mark Lwoff, Helsinki-based Bufo is behind such works as Aki Kaurismäki’s Berlinale Silver Bear Winner “The Other Side of Hope” and Cannes competition entry “Eagles of the Republic.” It’s moving “Something Rotten,” about a mixed-race Finnish man who believes his Libyan father abandoned him — until a video reveals the truth and unleashes a ghost, forcing him to face trauma and his own internalized racism.
	

	France

	Alice Perrault, Alabama ProductionAiming to move from shorts to full-length titles, such as Miriam Fürniss-Yacoubi’s “The Peter Principle,” her feature follow up to the 17-minute English-language “After The Very End,” a Carte Blanche Canal+ Clermont Ferrand winner. It turns on a couple of thirty-year-olds facing an existential crisis through the ironic prism of the Peter Principle: the higher people climb, the less competent they become. This “is the next step in our shared ambition to create bold, internationally driven auteur cinema,” says Perrault.

	Anne-Laure Berteau, Because the Night Productions



	

					‘Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance’
									Courtesy of Because the Night Productions
	



	Founded by Berteau in 2018, its credits taking in Isidore Bethel’s debut “Liam” (Tënk) and Louise Groult’s “Gertrude and Yvan Party Hard” (France Télévisions). Now moving “Behemoth Ann Holds a Seance,” a doc feature  remembering Arthur Douglas Thayer, who spent a lifetime crocheting creatures, shot by his wife, son and Daniel Hymanson as they organise an exhibition at the world’s busiest airport in Atlanta. “Shooting and editing become ways of rewriting their lives – of transforming sorrow into a story that transcends reality,” says Berteau.

	Gabriel Jumel, Belladone FilmsNormandy-based, behind auteur-driven fiction and documentary projects with strong social and political dimensions, such as Yannick Kergoat’s 2025 “Sarkozy-Gaddafi: The Scandal of All Scandals.” Now developing François-Xavier Rouyer’s “Half of the World,” about a fallen YouTube star who moves into an abandoned gated community in Switzerland and discovers she’s being watched by a mysterious intruder. A “contemporary genre film with elements of comedy, exploring surveillance, social media obsession, and the  constant search for online validation,” says Juhel. 

	Germany
	

	Alec Barth, Counterintuitive FilmBehind 2023 Locarno winner “Critical Zone” and 2026 Visions du Reel screener “Opera of Horror and Salvation,” the company aims for “artistically uncompromising feature films.” At Locarno with Sina Ataeian Dena’s “Foxperson,” about an animal rights activist who, after rescuing an injured fox in Paris, is compelled to cross a moral line that transforms both himself and the city. “‘Foxperson’ explores how binary thinking can polarize a society until extreme decisions become acceptable — both politically and personally,” Barth tells Variety. 

	Jasper Wiedhöft, Reynard Films



	

					‘Jo of Montreal’
									Courtesy of CMS
	



	Producer of Venice Days award-recipient “A Sad and Beautiful World” and the acclaimed “The Miserable Mother,” Reynard Films is partnering with Tabi360 and Creative Media Solutions on Ameen Nayfeh’s “Jo of Montreal,” about a spoiled 12-year-old gamer stranded in a remote Jordanian village. After meeting a shepherd, he rediscovers his roots and a passion for the village’s ancient heritage. The film offers a “universal theme of mentorship with a unique Levantine flavor,” says Nayfeh. It’s “Oscar-nominated ‘Theeb’ meets ‘Karate Kid,’ but without karate.”

	Melissa Byrne, Allergikerfilm, Nordpolaris



	

					‘The West Was Never Waiting’
									Courtesy of Allergikerfilm
	



	Repping Munich shingles Allergikerfilm and Nordpolaris, Melissa Byrne’s credits include Venice Critics’ Week opener “Life is Not a Competition, But I’m Winning” and Cannes Critics Week prize winner “‘Vaterland’ or a Bule Named Yanto.” At Match Me! she presents Justina Jürgensen’s “The West Was Never Waiting,” a female-led Western. Set amidst the greed of the 1860s gold rush, “the landscape becomes a state of mind and the action-packed journey into the Colorado wilderness unfolds as a descent into the human soul,” Jürgensen says.

	Italy

	Bruno Cristaldi, Eutropia FilmRome-based company Eutropia, headed by Bruno Cristaldi and Antonio Marzotto, aims to produce works that “inspire, provoke thought, and leave a lasting impact.” Current productions include upcoming docs “Reality is an Invitation” and “The Last Winner.” At Locarno, Eutropia presents “Manu e Vincenzina,” from  Alessandro Borrelli, which follows two sisters who dream of snow-capped mountains while on the run from a Naples juvenile center. “A road movie about survival, sisterhood, and the fragile border between danger and hope,” they say.

	Camilla Gazzola, Amartia Film
	



	

					‘Reborn’
									Courtesy of Amartia Film
	



	Rome and Naples-based and behind Leone Balduzzi’s 2024 feature doc “Sting Like a Bee,” Amartia is moving “Reborn,” Francesco Pascucci’s doc feature made with Belgium’s Harald House and winner of a MIA Development Award and Italy’s 2025 Doc/it Women Award. It depicts a community of women forming deep emotional bonds with hyper-realistic silicone dolls resembling newborns. It asks a difficult question, Gazzola says. “What happens when our need for connection finds its answer in something that cannot respond?”

	Salvatore Lizzio, RevokSpecializing in auteurist international co-productions, Revok’s recent productions include Giovanni C. Lorusso’s “Homo Sive Natura” and Marcello Di Noto’s “Pazzo & Bella.” At Locarno with Lorusso’s “Despite Evil” (“Malgré le mal”), about an elderly couple in La Reunión’s remote mountains waiting for a doctor impeded by an approaching cyclone. Facing their final farewell, they look back on their shared life. It’s an “intimate portrayal of love, loss, and mortality, told through visually powerful and emotionally restrained cinematic language,” says Lizzio.

	Latvia

	Grēta Grebže, Tasse FilmRiga-based Tasse Film, best known for Berlinale Crystal Bear winner “Mellow Mud” and hit series “Soviet Jeans,” arrives in Locarno with Alise Zarina’s “Not My War.” It follows Lote, a young woman preparing for motherhood, but when war breaks out across the border, her carefully planned life is suddenly disrupted. “The main themes are the uncertainty we learn to live with, women in war as sort of outcasts and the future my generation faces in these turbulent times,” says Zarina.

	Līva Vernere, VFS Films



	

					‘In The Truth’
									Credit: Toms Harjo
	



	VFS Films boasts an award-winning slate of titles and international co-productions, including acclaimed docs “Bridges of Time” and “Redlight to Limelight.” At Locarno with Toms Harjo’s “In The Truth,” co-produced by Les Films d’Antoine. It follows 17-year-old Tom as he struggles to satisfy both his strict Jehovah’s Witness family and his own emerging sexual desires. Drawing from Harjo’s own experiences, it examines “a rarely seen religious community with intimacy and nuance” while “revealing the profoundly human desire to belong,” says Vernere.

	Lithuania
	

	Viktorija Rimkutė, Dansu Films



	

					‘The Queen Of England Stole My Parents’
									Courtesy of Dansu Films
	



	One of Lithuania’s biggest producers, co-producing “Agent Hamilton” and “Solomamma” and producing “Troll Farm,” at 2025’s Berlinale Series Market Selects. Now priming Ernestas Jankauskas’ “The Queen Of England Stole My Parents,” a semi fantasy fable exploring the challenges faced by foster parents when adopting Smiltė, a 10-year-old rebel with a vivid imagination. A Tallinn Co-Production Market favorite pitch award winner. 

	Akvilė Žilionytė, ArtišokaiDeveloping documentary and fiction films rooted in personal stories with international relevance. Its first doc-feature, “In Passing,” premiered in 2025. Teaming with Poland’s MX35 on Nuruzzaman Khan’s “Where It Rains,” co-written by Žilionytė, about a Bangladeshi father living in Lithuania writing letters to his son, trying to bridge the distance between two cultures and two homes. “At first, I thought I was making a film to preserve my son’s childhood. Somewhere along the way, I realised I was also trying to preserve my own,” says Khan.

	Montenegro

	Ivan Marinović, Adriatic Western



	

					Nikola Đuričko stars in ‘The Educator’
									Credit: Milan Josipović/Adriatic Western
	



	Founded by Ivan Marinović, Adriatic Western is behind award-winning films “The Black Pin” and “Forever Hold Your Peace.” At Locarno with “The Educator,” produced with Sense Production, a body-horror comedy about a teacher who remains drunk to suppress his inner monster. Chaos ensures when his pupil discovers the truth. It’s “a fresh take on the Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde myth,” exploring “what childhood feels like when the people meant to educate and protect you become the source of fear,” Marinović says. 

	Miljan Vučelić, Protos FilmProtos Film, headed by Miljan Vučelić, focuses on author-driven works, supports emerging filmmakers and develops projects with strong international potential. Recent features include “Comedown,” currently in post, and doc “About a Brother.” At Locarno with Đorđe Vojvodić’s development prize-winning “Nothing Will Be Named After Me,” produced with Bitter Frames, about a once powerful state official recovering from a stroke in his luxury hotel but trying desperately to retain power. It “moves from darkly comic character drama into psychological thriller,” Vučelić teases.

	Poland
	

	Julia Jendrysik, Rizz Films



	

					‘Mother Daughter’
									Courtesy of Rizz Films
	



	Warsaw-based Rizz Films, headed by Julia Jendrysik and Anna Majek, develops local works and international co-productions, including Tomasz Wróbel’s Fantasia short “The Noise of Waves.” It presents at Match Me! “Mother Daughter,” co-produced with WFDiF. Based on Mira Marcinów’s acclaimed novel, the film follows Rita, who’s forced to confront memories and trauma when her mother suddenly falls ill. While it explores difficult family themes “and the complexity of the mother-daughter relationship, it never loses its sense of humor,” Jendrysik tells Variety.

	Richard Karpala, Latarka StudioLatarka Studio, launched by Richard Karpala, saw debut film “Falling Stars” premiere at Locarno, where it’s now moving “Lektor.” About a foreign film voice-over narrator who, after the fall of communism, begins hearing his own voice in every foreigner he encounters. Now jobless, he discovers it’s an unexpected asset abroad. Focusing on a dubber was ideal “for a story set in the early ’90s” about a man who “has to adapt to the cultural and economic changes happening around him,” Karbala says.

	Korek Bojanowski, AmondoA Warsaw-based collective producing films and international co-productions,” Amondo is behind Warsaw screener “Hel” and Venice entry “The Hole in the Fence.” At Locarno with Bojanowski’s “The Art of Spitting.” Warsaw’s only superhero, Julek can fly but has never saved a single life. When a disastrous encounter is mistaken for a heroic rescue, he decides to expose the truth and the charade that is his life. “A portrait of millennial disappointment, wounded masculinity and the need to feel exceptional,” says Bojanowski. 

	Portugal

	Ana Sofia Nunes, Jângal Studios“Focusing on emerging directors, with particular attention to new forms of storytelling and a commitment to diverse and distinctive voices,” says Nunes. Now developing “Capricorn Syndrome,” (“Síndrome de Capricórnio”), one of its first international co-productions, with Portugal’s David & Golias and Finland’s Films Films Films, “framing mental illness within a dystopian yet familiar reality, the film reflects on our growing search for certainty in an increasingly unstable world,” says director Miguel Munhá. 

	Ana Almeida, MatinéBehind “Terra Vil,” its debut feature, a Tallinn Black Nights competition contender which closed distribution deals for Spain and The Netherlands, besides the production countries Portugal and Italy. Now backing murder mystery “Sacrifice Hill,” adapting Antonio Muñoz Molina’s same-titled short story, “a tense, serene and mysterious film noir,” says its director Luis Filipe Rocha, a 2017 Portuguese Academy Award original screenplay winner for “Grey and Black.”  
	

	Spain

	David Aymerich, Ayhe ProductionsTarragona-based, founded in 2020, behind divorce drama “March 14,” and making ambitious strong-identity auteur-driven films from a new generation of filmmakers. At Match Me! with “Cara Sucia,” about Bruno, a Black teenager, marked by skin vitiligo, sentenced to work at a residential home for minors with functional diversity. Unexpectedly, he finds a safe place where he can accept himself by embracing others. “A special coming-of-age story portraying a reality rarely seen on screen,” Aymerich says. 

	Eva Bodas, Entre las PiedrasOne of Variety’s 2024 10 Emerging Spanish Producers, founding Madrid-based Entre las Piedras in 2022, “to produce bold, political films and giving voice to new filmmaker generations.” She hits Match Me! with “Laguna The Minister,” Antonio Llamas’ follow-up to DocumentaMadrid Audience Award winner “A Suburban Mythology.” An Atlántida – Mallorca Talents Lab laureate turning on a government minister who suddenly stops taking orders and disappear, it “addresses the visceral dissatisfaction with those who make decisions,” says Llamas.

	Jesús Chora Zataraín, Lazona ZinemaHeading up Lazona Zinema, the Basque division of Lazona (“Spanish Affair,” “Gigantes”), which aims to “produce bold, risk-taking projects from emerging Basque voices and also large-scale productions and international co-productions,” he says. At Locarno with a banner new talent project, Ikusmira Berriak winner “La Koreana,” Basque writer-director Joana Moya feature debut, produced with Sirimiri Films, founded by Estibaliz Urresola, director of Berlinale winner “20,000 Species of Bees.” Another of Variety’s 2024 10 Emerging Spanish Producers.

title: Toni Braxton Resolves 6-Figure Tax Lien Years After Bankruptcy
description:
Toni Braxton

                          Y
body:
Toni Braxton
                          Resolves 6-Figure Tax Lien ...
                          Years After Bankruptcy Battle
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 7, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 7, 2026
                                4:29 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Toni Braxton says she settled a debt with the IRS … over a decade after she finalized her second bankruptcy.
      
    
            According to official records, the singer was hit with a federal tax lien on June 22 ... and Uncle Sam said she owed A LOT of money.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The breakdown of the debt is $69,390 for 2022, $278,876 for 2023, and $250,358 for 2024 ... totaling around $598K.
      
    
            A rep for Toni tells TMZ the singer resolved the bill.  
      

            As TMZ previously reported, the "Braxton Family Values" star filed for bankruptcy in 1998 after a battle over money with her record label.
      
    
            The singer was criticized heavily for her debt … and was even scolded by Oprah during an episode of her talk show. 
      
    
            Toni's money problems arose again in 2010, when she filed for bankruptcy a second time, claiming she owed millions to creditors. 
      
    
            The second bankruptcy was closed in 2015.

title: Universal Studios Hollywood Guests Warned After Measles Exposure
description:
Universal Studios Hollywood
                          Infected Visitor Triggers Measles Warning
body:
Universal Studios Hollywood
                          Infected Visitor Triggers Measles Warning
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 6, 2026
                            6:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Universal Studios Hollywood guests are being urged to check their vaccination status after a person infected with measles visited the theme park last month ... potentially putting others at risk.
      
    
            The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health says the infected visitor was at Universal on July 26. Anyone who was inside the park from 10 AM to 9 PM that day is being advised to make sure they’re protected and watch closely for possible symptoms through August 16.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A Universal Studios Hollywood spokesperson tells TMZ ... "The safety and security of our guests and team members is our highest priority. We were recently made aware that a guest with a confirmed case of measles visited Los Angeles County, including our theme park, on July 26, 2026. We are working with the Department of Public Health and are following their guidance."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Measles can spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and the virus can remain in an area for up to two hours. Symptoms include fever, a cough, runny nose, red eyes and a rash.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Dana Bash turned CNN’s "State of the Union" into a heated debate Sunday, with the HHS secretary and the anchor clashing over the measles, COVID, vaccines, public health, and autism research.
      
    
            During the interview, Bash urged Kennedy to use his platform to encourage parents to vaccinate their children. Kennedy eventually looked into the camera and delivered a message encouraging parents to vaccinate against measles ... but not without some begging from Bash.
      
    
            The alert from The L.A. County Department of Public Health comes as measles cases surge nationwide. More than 2,300 infections have been reported in the U.S. this year, marking the highest annual total since 1991.
